beta_new: Climbed by Sam Boyce and Kyle Willis in July 2018 as part of a four-day 'Boston Marathon' link-up; they knew of no previously published complete west-to-east crossing. From Sibley Pass, a faint climbers' trail (generally used to access Marble Creek Basin) leads along the ridge; the route then tags West, Middle, and East Triad in sequence along the crest. The west face of Middle Triad has the best rock on the route and holds the technical crux at 5.6 R; elsewhere the ridge is serious, exposed 4th-class and low-5th-class scrambling on generally poor ('choss') rock. A separate 2018 descent of the East Ridge toward the Eldorado Glacier involved pushing past large loose blocks and roughly 500 ft of very exposed 5.6–5.7 downclimbing to reach the glacier.

Shares its first pitch with the Northwest Corner up a dirty face/chimney to a huge sandy ledge, then follows a steep right-facing corner, a lieback flake with an airy step past a bolt, and a sustained undercling/lieback corner crack into the crux: a thin tips crack that eases into easier ground higher up, finishing on lower-angle crack and slab climbing.

Parties typically combine this with the South Peak lookout climb in a single trip since both share the same long approach. From Camp Saddle/Tin Can Gap, descend onto the glacier and traverse to the base of the North Peak, then climb the West Couloir to the South Face. One party describes the climbing as Class 4 with one Class 5 move in the chimney, then easing to Class 2 and 3 near the summit — easier than it is sometimes described, with rock character compared to Chimney Rock.

The Middle Peak is climbed far less often than the South Peak (lookout) or North Peak and has very little published route detail; it shares the same long Goat Flats/Tin Can Gap approach as the other two summits before diverging toward the Middle Peak's south side. Treat any attempt as a serious, lightly-documented alpine rock objective and be prepared to route-find.

This is the line Harry Bedal, Harold Engles, and Frank Benesh used to reach the South Peak summit to build the fire lookout in the early 1930s, and it remains the standard way up. From the trailhead the route follows trail to Saddle Lake, Goat Flats, and Tin Can Gap, then crosses the edge of the Queest-Alb Glacier before a rock scramble and a set of three fixed ladders (rebar and timber anchored into steep rock) gain the summit block and lookout. It is popular as a long day trip or, more commonly, an overnight from Goat Flats or Tin Can Gap given the approach length.

The talus steepens toward the Main-Middle notch, which is marked by a chockstone; from there the line traverses a broad south-facing ledge to a rock gable roughly 150 ft below the summit, then climbs a solid, enjoyable class 4 chimney directly to the top.

moves.from: From the Mineral Creek Trailhead, the route follows the Mineral Creek trail before heading off-trail through brush to the base of a long talus slope on Middle Peak's south side.

beta_new: From the Mineral Creek Trail, leave the tread west of the broad waterfall gully and climb off-trail through vine maple and then long south-side talus and scree to the southeast shoulder (about 6,200 ft). From the shoulder, traverse roughly a quarter mile of steep snow or talus onto the northeast ridge, then scramble the final ~400 ft up the ridge to the East (true) summit. The step onto the ridge and the upper ridge are loose, exposed class 3 with a short class 4 move or two, so test every hold. A separate, longer line from a camp at Upper Park Lake climbs the north side to the Main-Middle notch and crosses a ledge system on the north face; it is a different route, not part of this one.

After camping at Spectacle Point (5,800 ft), the route climbs the West Ridge and West Face of West Peak to the summit — a mix of rock scrambling and rock climbing, i.e. class 3-4 terrain without a documented technical crux comparable to the Middle Peak chimney.

From the Yellow Aster Butte/Tomyhoi Lake Trailhead, follow maintained trail up to the high meadows and tarns below Yellow Aster Butte (~5,580 ft), then leave the trail and head NNW over a hump to a col (~6,266 ft). Climb the broadening ridge (Tomyhoi Arm); where it narrows, bypass on broad benches on the north side, then traverse the top of the Tomyhoi Glacier to avoid rock pinnacles lower on the ridge. Cross a moat/notch below the final summit pyramid (hard snow, ice axe useful) and finish with a delightful but exposed Class 3 scramble on solid rock to the true summit; one party describes a V-shaped Class 3.5 slot near the top that some parties belay or lower packs through, especially on descent.

Seven-pitch, 800-ft Grade IV 5.12a on the east side of the tower. The route alternates bolt-protected technical slab pitches (P1, P2, P5) with crack pitches (P3, P4, P6-P7) that need a full trad rack. Rock quality is noted as inconsistent, with looser sections on P1 and the P4 roof traverse.

moves.from: Descent is either a rappel of the route with two 70m ropes, or an exposed 4th-class traverse west from the East Shoulder to the same gully used by East Face parties.

beta_new: Start up any of the standard routes on The Tooth (most parties use the South Face) to reach its summit, then follow the crest toward Chair Peak. The traverse mixes exposed 4th/low-5th-class scrambling and climbing on generally sub-par rock, with a short section of forest walking after leaving The Tooth, and one mandatory ~50-ft rappel off Bryant Peak partway along.

Lead Sidewinder, then lower from its chains to the lip of the roof; from there, toprope back up through steep, technical moves to the shared anchor. Only about 30 ft, but sustained and powerful for the grade.

A more moderate alpine alternative to the North Tower Ridge Route, following an exciting arete with great exposure but lower technical difficulty. Route can be split into two parts: approach on easier terrain, then a more dramatic arete section. Requires careful attention to loose rock and boulders throughout. Approximately 4-5 hour total time from campground.

Climbed in the 1970s by John Roper, Don Avreitt, and Stu Ferguson; first skied in 2012 by Rowan Stewart and Alex Spoonde. Reached via Cascade Pass (or the nearby 'Alliteration Col') and a descent to Trapper Lake, the couloir is booted or skinned/booted from the lake basin, with ascent plates or crampons typically needed on firm crust higher up. Documented ascents run from January (icy) through late June (near-solstice corn/graupel), most commonly climbed/skied April-May.

From the Stevens Pass Ski Area, climb the service road/trail past Skyline Lake to a gap in Skyline Ridge, then descend the ridge's north/back side into a creek drainage before climbing back up to gain Tye Peak's south ridge, which leads to the summit. There is no maintained trail; the route is class 2 terrain but requires route-finding and, outside of firm snow cover, pushing through dense brush. Tye Peak and neighboring Sky Mountain share the same approach and are often combined in one trip.

Eight pitches climb twin cracks, a chimney/right-facing corner, delicate face moves, and a bulging, thin-corner roof-traverse crux (P4, 5.11a) before wide cracks and chimneys and a final hand-crack/offwidth pitch reach the summit. Described by climbers as a good route that would be excellent with more traffic; some sections (notably the P6 corner) were noted as lichen-covered/dirty as of a 2018 ascent.

moves.from: From Burgundy Col, descend around the north face to a twin-crack system with obvious loose blocks about 60 ft up (Action Potential's start is roughly 15 ft to the left).

beta_new: From the Smithbrook Road trailhead, hike the Smithbrook Trail roughly 0.9 mile up through old-growth forest to its junction with the Pacific Crest Trail near Union Gap. Leave the trail after a short distance and bushwhack northeast to gain Union Peak's southeast ridge at about 5,200 ft, then follow the ridge to the 5,696-5,700 ft summit. The line is an easy-to-moderate, non-technical alpine scramble in summer/fall and a moderate winter scramble or backcountry ski/snowshoe objective the rest of the year.

The Castle is a spire north of the main Dikes climbing area, with two bolted climbs to its top. Rock quality is poor and the approach is a bushwhack/scramble, but the exposure and summit view are notable.
Bolted sport route in the Alpenkuhl area. Quality granite with good rock and solid protection.
Bolted sport route in the Alpenkuhl area. Solid granite with excellent rock quality; steeper terrain.
Bolted sport route in the Alpenkuhl area. Clean granite with excellent rock quality; popular route.
Trad climbing route in the Alpenkuhl area using natural protection and gear. Solid granite with good structure for placing protection.
Bolted sport route in the Alpenkuhl area. Good granite with excellent rock quality.

Six sustained pitches of corners and cracks, climbed all free, up a sunny, southwest-facing wall; the hardest climbing is on pitch one. Three fixed protection bolts and one bolted anchor supplement gear. The route earned a 3-star rating in its first documented ascents.

Grade IV, 5.9. Eleven pitches of low/mid 5th class (5.5-5.6) to Great Gendarme; two crux pitches of 5.9 on the Gendarme itself (steep hand/finger dihedral and offwidth requiring 3.5 protection). Hazards: knife-edge ridge with 1,000+ feet of exposure, loose rock, variable snow/ice conditions, wet terrain mid-ridge, cold wind on exposed ridge, rockfall from climber traffic, steep descent terrain. Requires advanced alpine rock climbing skills, crack protection (especially 3.5"), excellent weather judgment, overnight bivy capability. Total climbing time: 16-20 hours car-to-car. Best months: June-August (snow dependent).

Vanishing Point is approximately as steep a route as one could find on the mountain—sustained, largely overhanging climbing, with most pitches at 5.11–5.12 and several at 5.10. The route was established over several years and fully modernized in 2020 with new stainless-steel anchors and improved protection. Notable features include the crux 5.12 pitch out a huge roof (pitch 11), a collapsed roof section, and several intentionally runout pitches. Published pitch counts vary between 14 and 20 depending on how the climbing is split or linked; the pitch-by-pitch breakdown here uses the 14-pitch convention.

moves.from: The approach involves 800 feet of mostly roped-up slab climbing with fixed lines and bolts.

beta_new: This is the standard line up the ridge's true high point, first climbed by Fred Beckey and Herb Staley in 1952. From Burgundy Col, work north along/just below the ridge crest on 4th-class rock to a notch on the north side of the summit block, then scramble south around the west side of a large summit boulder to the base of a short low-5th-class step that gains the true summit. Most parties do it as a long day from the Washington Pass pullout, and many combine it with the neighboring Acropolis and Niki Tower to the south for an efficient multi-summit day on the ridge.

moves.from: An old fixed rappel anchor sits at the top for the descent.

beta_new: Ascend along the SW spur, heading east to a broken ledge with a tree on the left. Climb up and left over a short slab to a notch, then through the notch and along a terraced ledge to a gully on the crest of the SW spur. Continue along the scree terrace below the summit block, then descend to the prominent tree visible from the road and climb the long crack to the summit.

This is the primary route to Warrior Peak's Southeast Summit. From the cirque below the peak, ascend the obvious couloir between the SE and NW summits. If snow-filled (common early season), the couloir is steep and straightforward; if melted out, it's loose scree. Above the couloir, scramble to a saddle at approximately 7,000 feet, then climb steep snow or a snow moat to reach the exposed rock section. Some parties rope this short pitch; others solo it depending on conditions and skill.

moves.from: The route involves approximately 9-10 miles of approach hiking, making it a typical 2-day backpacking objective.
moves.value: Plan on roughly 9-10 miles of hiking to reach the base of the climb, which makes this a typical two-day backpacking objective.

beta_new: From Washington's summit, follow the narrow crest of fractured pillow basalt southwest toward Ellinor. The initial 'Wedge' gives about 150 ft of positive, low-5th/class-4 climbing — the best section on the route. Beyond it the ridge continues as sustained class-4 scrambling past a series of gendarmes (hidden ledges usually keep difficulty at class 4 or below), with one loose ~50 ft downclimb considered the least enjoyable section. Where the ridge gets too difficult or exposed to continue unroped, most parties drop into the basin below and either downclimb a technical sequence or bypass it on a snow finger to rejoin Ellinor's standard winter route to that summit. An alternative some parties recommend over the direct ridge: the standard west-side basin traverse into Ellinor's NE couloir.

Ascends the rib left of Roan Wall's major slab waterfall, which gives the route some protection from snow/debris shed from above — though the base is still commonly buried under residual avalanche snow for much of the climbing season. Facing east, it gets direct morning sun and afternoon shade. Climbing is a varied mix of bolted face and mostly-thin cracks; described as a modern Darrington-area classic with some climbing more reminiscent of Index or Yosemite than typical Darrington granite.

Approach via the Copper Glance Trail to Copper Glance Lake and the upper basin below Isabella Ridge, camp or day-trip from there, then ascend talus/scree and a south-facing gully to the south ridge and follow it to the summit. Commonly combined with an ascent of neighboring Big Craggy Peak (connected by a ridge/saddle) in the same trip. Loose rock (choss) and lingering snow in the gully are the main technical considerations; route is class 2 with brief class 2-3 scrambling in places.

A premier alpine testpiece featuring five pitches of high-quality granite climbing to the summit terrace, plus a short sixth pitch up an easy chimney to the summit. The route climbs splitter cracks and exposed face climbing over 600 vertical feet. Pitch 2 contains the crux with thin cracks, bulbous knobs, and a small roof. The climbing features varied terrain including incipient flakes, stemming, and lieback sections. Protection is generally reliable on white granite. The onsight first free ascent in 2007 was completed with no falls.

moves.from: Descent via four double-rope rappels from the summit.

beta_new: A hidden-gem moderate that has become cleaner and more popular over the years. The line rambles up cracks and the ridge crest with sustained mid-fifth-class climbing throughout; the crux comes about halfway up, on pitch 4, on a short section of steep twin finger cracks, and the final pitch is an exposed, runout 5.8 face regarded by many parties as the route's real ("mental") crux. Often camped for and combined with the North Face of Burgundy Spire for a ~12-13 pitch link-up day.

Approached from a multi-day camp in Crescent Creek Basin (reached via the Goodell Creek / Terror Creek / Barrier approach), the route crosses roughly a mile of basin terrain before climbing a chockstone-filled gully system rated up to 5.7 (also given as South Face, Grade II, 5th class). Loose rock and route-finding are the main challenges; parties commonly climb this as a side objective from a Southern Pickets base camp rather than a stand-alone trailhead-to-summit day.

Pitch 2 is a lieback/stemming crux; pitch 3 is a delicate smearing finger traverse; the upper two pitches ease into pleasant smearing and cruising to the top. Protection mixes hand-drilled bolts on the faces with gear in the dihedral/crack sections.

Follow the north ridge, which dips slightly in places, to the summit pyramid. There the rock opens into many possible lines; keeping to the north (right-hand) side is easier, and there are rappel slings on the far side. Expect loose rock and choose lines carefully.

moves.from: Pick up the climbers' trail from the pullout, cross the basin and gain the notch between Whistler and Cutthroat.
moves.value: From the pullout, follow the climbers' trail across the basin to the notch between Whistler and Cutthroat, where the north ridge begins.

beta_new: From a roadside turnout on SR-20 (or alternatively the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead), a boot path climbs through open forest and a meadow basin, then rises on a traversing line to intersect the level part of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft. From there the route follows the ridge and adjoining gullies — staying north of a loose gully band and using a visible ramp near the headwall — to the 7,790 ft summit; an alternative continues the ridge to about 6,800 ft before cutting left across gullies onto gentler terrain on the southwest slope for the final push. It is class 3 scrambling throughout, with class 4 moves possible depending on line choice.

This is a remote, non-technical scramble whose difficulty is really the approach: roughly 15-17 miles of biking/hiking one-way just to reach camp near Anderson Pass, followed by an 8-mile round-trip, ~4,000 ft scramble day with no maintained trail above the pass. The summit push itself is rated Class 2. There is no record of a notable first ascent or established named line — it is climbed as a cross-country objective, not a route in the rock-climbing sense.

Begin on Niederprum Trail #953/653, which quickly degenerates into a steep, brushy boot path climbing to an alpine bench near the old Niederprum mine. Continue on snow to Lone Tree Pass (~4,900 ft; the 'lone tree' is actually a cluster of three trees, not at the pass), traverse below the northwest ridge to High Pass (~6,000-6,030 ft), cross onto the Whitehorse Glacier, and climb a snow/ice ridge to the base of the summit block, finishing with exposed Class 3 scrambling to the true summit.

Early in the season, roughly April to June, the same line is climbed as a continuous snow and ice route. Parties stay on snow higher on the shoulder and face instead of threading the rock bands that appear later, keep climber's right on the glacier to avoid the worst crevassing, and meet a steep, sometimes icy rollover of about 50-55 degrees, the crux in these conditions. It is a popular ski and splitboard objective: many skin or boot the glacier basin and switch to crampons only for the final steep pitch below the summit, then ski back toward High Pass and Lone Tree Pass. Once deep snow has buried the brush, some parties go more directly up Snow Gulch from near the trailhead and stash skis around 2,500 ft for the descent.
